Over the past fifty years, cities around the world have grown at an

rate. In 1950, fewer than one third of the world's population lived in urban areas; today, more than half do. Many people move to cities in search of better jobs, higher wages and access to quality education and healthcare. Large cities also offer entertainment, cultural activities and a wide variety of services that rural areas rarely provide.

However, rapid urbanisation brings serious problems. Housing becomes expensive, and many newcomers have to live in overcrowded neighbourhoods. Traffic jams and air pollution affect the daily lives of millions of residents. To cope with these challenges, some governments are investing in public transport, building affordable housing and creating more green spaces. Experts believe that careful planning is the key to making cities liveable for everyone.

Sleep is as important to our health as food and exercise, yet many people do not get enough of

. Adults generally need between seven and nine hours of sleep each night, while teenagers require even more because their bodies are still developing. During sleep, the brain organises memories and the body repairs itself. People who regularly sleep too little often find it difficult to concentrate and are more likely to feel stressed.

Unfortunately, modern habits make good sleep harder to achieve. Many people use smartphones or watch television late at night, and the bright light from these screens can delay the production of the hormone that makes us sleepy. Doctors therefore advise going to bed at a regular time, avoiding caffeine in the evening and keeping the bedroom quiet and dark. Small changes like these can considerably improve both the quality and length of our sleep.
